opus-5.5.text:
Researchers, especially really talented ones, tend to have strong ideas about what they want to work on, and that's part of what makes them great. If you just put a bunch of brilliant people in a room and say "go collaborate," you usually don't get collaboration. You get a lot of individual projects that happen to sit near each other.

What I've found works is giving people a shared goal that's ambitious enough that no one person can accomplish it alone. When the goal is big enough, like training a model that does something nobody has done before, people naturally start depending on each other. The person working on data needs the person working on infrastructure, who needs the person working on evaluation. Collaboration becomes the only way to win, not a value you preach.

The second thing is being thoughtful about credit. Researchers care a lot about recognition, and rightly so, since their careers are built on it. On large projects, people worry they'll become a cog and their contributions will disappear. So you have to make sure that work which enables everyone else, the infrastructure, the tooling, the careful data work, is recognized and celebrated as much as the flashy result at the end.

Third, you need researchers with a certain kind of taste and temperament: people who care more about the result than about whose idea it was. In hiring, you can often tell who gets energy from other people's progress and who sees it as competition. You want the first kind.

Finally, leadership has to make the hard calls about focus. Part of making collaboration work is saying no to a lot of interesting directions so the team can concentrate on the few that matter. That's often uncomfortable, but if everyone is pulling in different directions, even the best people can't get anything big done.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to understand is that research is fundamentally a creative act, and you can't manage it the way you'd manage an engineering team. You can't say, "here's the roadmap, go build it." The thing you're actually trying to do is take a lot of very smart, very opinionated people and get them pointed at the same problem without killing the independence that makes them good in the first place.

The way I think about it is that you need a really clear, shared sense of what the mission is, and then you need to give people a lot of latitude on how they get there. At OpenAI, the thing that held everything together was that everyone genuinely believed we were trying to build AGI, and that the path ran through scale. Once you have that kind of north star, a lot of the coordination problems get easier, because people can make local decisions and they tend to point in the same direction.

The second thing is that you have to be honest about what's working. One of the biggest failure modes in a research lab is that people fall in love with their own ideas. Everybody has a pet direction. And the hard part of running a lab is creating a culture where it's okay to say, "this isn't working, let's consolidate behind the thing that is." That's really painful, because you're asking people to give up on something they care about. But if you look at the history of the big breakthroughs, a lot of them came from the moment where the organization stopped spreading its bets and said, we're going to put everything behind this one approach. GPT is a good example of that.

And then the last piece, which I think people underrate, is that you need a mix of people. You need the pure researchers who are going to go off and have the weird idea nobody else believes in. But you also need people who are willing to do the unglamorous engineering work that actually makes the research possible, the infrastructure, the data pipelines, the evaluation. The labs that work well are the ones where those two groups respect each other, where the engineers are treated as first-class contributors and not as support staff. If you can get that right, the rest tends to follow.

astra-6.text:
I think you start by recognizing that talented researchers need room to pursue their own ideas. You can’t organize research entirely from the top down, because part of the job is discovering which questions are worth asking. But if everyone is pursuing something independently, you lose a lot of the benefit of having a lab.

So the balance is to give people a shared sense of what matters and then a lot of freedom in how they approach it. What are we trying to accomplish? What are the big uncertainties? Where would progress unlock other work? Those are useful conversations for leadership to facilitate.

Then you want to make it easy for researchers to learn from one another. That means sharing early results, being comfortable talking about things that didn’t work, and giving people credit for helping someone else succeed. Ideally, collaboration isn’t something you have to mandate. People do it because working together helps them make more progress on the problems they care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give people a shared sense of what they’re trying to accomplish, while leaving them a lot of freedom in how they get there. Talented researchers usually have strong intuitions about what’s worth pursuing. You want to make room for that, and also make it easy for them to find collaborators whose strengths complement their own.

A lot of the work is creating an environment where people share results early, including things that didn’t work, and can challenge each other’s ideas without making it personal. You can’t really dictate which research ideas will succeed. But you can help people understand the bigger picture, put good teams together, and make sure that when someone discovers something promising, the organization can get behind it.
